deep.reconstruction:
Setting: a spherical triangle with sides a, b, c and opposite angles A, B, C (a triangle is sketched on the previous page). The next page lists the four Gauss–Delambre analogies. This page is a scratch step toward them, starting from the five-part (analogue) formulas. The first two formulas are my reconstruction; they are not written on the page:
  sin a cos B = cos b sin c − sin b cos c cos A
  sin a cos C = cos c sin b − sin c cos b cos A.

(1) ADDING them (my step) gives sin a (cos B + cos C) = (sin c cos b + cos c sin b) − cos A (sin b cos c + cos b sin c). This is exactly the first written line, sin(b+c) − cos A sin(b+c). The second line factors it: = (1 − cos A) sin(b+c).

(2) SUBTRACTING them (my step) gives sin a (cos C − cos B) = (sin b cos c − cos b sin c) + cos A (sin b cos c − cos b sin c). This is the third written line, sin(b−c) + sin(b−c) cos A. The obvious completion, = (1 + cos A) sin(b−c), is not written.

Purpose (my completion of the route): rewrite the left sides with sum-to-product formulas:
  cos B + cos C = 2 cos½(B+C) cos½(B−C)
  cos C − cos B = 2 sin½(B+C) sin½(B−C).
Rewrite the right sides with 1 − cos A = 2 sin²½A, 1 + cos A = 2 cos²½A and sin(b±c) = 2 sin½(b±c) cos½(b±c). Combining with the sine rule (and the companion half-angle relations) yields the four analogies on the next page, e.g. sin½A cos½(b+c) = cos½a cos½(B+C) and sin½A sin½(b+c) = sin½a cos½(B−C). Taking the ratio of the two results gives cot½(B+C) cot½(B−C) = tan²½A · sin(b+c)/sin(b−c).
errors: No errors in the written steps. The page is incomplete: the right-hand side of the third line, (1+cos A) sin(b−c), is never written down.
The left-hand sides, sin a (cos B ± cos C), are only implicit; the page shows just the right-hand sides of the summed and differenced five-part formulas.

results.what: Sum and difference of the spherical five-part formulas: sin a (cos B + cos C) = (1 − cos A) sin(b+c) and sin a (cos C − cos B) = (1 + cos A) sin(b−c)
results.modern_name: Spherical analogue (five-part) formulas; intermediate step in deriving the Delambre (Gauss) analogies
results.usually_credited_to: Five-part formulas: classical (Euler/Lagrange era). The analogies: Delambre (1807), Mollweide (1808), Gauss (Theoria motus, 1809)

results.what: Context: half-angle relations leading to the four analogies (written on the next page)

deep.surprise_reason: This is elementary trigonometric factoring in service of the Gauss–Delambre analogies, which Gauss published in Theoria motus (1809). It is routine scratch work.

checkable.asserts: Adding the two five-part formulas gives line 1, i.e. sin a (cos B + cos C).
Subtracting the two five-part formulas gives line 3, i.e. sin a (cos C − cos B).
Half-angle form used to reach the analogies.

transcription_corrections: The transcription is essentially correct. The first line reads sin(b+c) − cos A sin(b+c); the first sin(b+c) is written faintly.
Line 3 has no right-hand side on the page; the implied completion is (1+cos A) sin(b−c).
The large pencil 'N' at the bottom is probably a sorting or library mark, not mathematics.
